---
title: "Quiz: generating and exploring images with a VAE"
---

Short questions on generating, interpolating and using a trained VAE. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** How do you generate a new image with a trained VAE?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which part of the network do you need, and where does its input come from?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Draw $z$ from the prior $\mathcal N(0, I)$ and pass it through the decoder. The encoder is not needed.
:::

---

**Q2.** True or false: the latent midpoint of two images always decodes to the pixel average of the two images.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
True for a linear decoder. Is the VAE decoder linear?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
False. A linear decoder (PCA) maps the midpoint to the average, a double exposure. A curved decoder maps it to an in-between **shape**: a bar halfway, a digit halfway between a 1 and a 7.
:::

---

**Q3.** A colleague names the latent axes of a 2D VAE "$z_1$ = thickness" and "$z_2$ = slant". What is the problem?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does the loss change if the latent space is rotated?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The prior $\mathcal N(0, I)$ and the KL penalty look the same after a rotation of the latent space, so the axes have no fixed meaning; another training run could give rotated or flipped axes. Directions should be read from decoded images along them, and need not line up with the axes.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why are the images from a VAE blurrier than the training images?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What single image best matches several different images in squared error?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Several training images share each region of latent space, and the decoder outputs one image for it. The output that minimises the average squared error is their average, and an average of slightly different sharp images is blurred.
:::

---

**Q5.** You use reconstruction error to find unusual cells. Name one kind of unusual cell this will catch and one it may miss.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What can the decoder draw?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It catches shapes the decoder cannot draw (a ring, two cells in one crop: large error). It misses unusual cells that happen to look like a normal one in squared error (a square close to a round cell), and small details that change few pixels.
:::

---

**Q6.** What does increasing $\beta$ do to generated images and to the latent space?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Stronger pull towards the prior.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The latent space gets smoother and better filled, with directions that often follow one factor each; the images get blurrier and more average.
:::
